Bats are the only mammals that can truly fly, and many of them hunt at night. To find their way in the dark, most bats use a skill called echolocation. A bat makes high squeaks that are too high for people to hear. The sound bounces off trees, walls, and insects, and the echoes travel back to the bat's large ears. From these echoes, the bat can tell how far away something is and even how big it is.

I once watched bats swoop over the pond near my grandmother's house in Ohio. They darted, turned, and dove faster than I could follow. A single bat can eat hundreds of insects in one night, so farmers are often glad to have them nearby.

A honeybee colony is like a small, busy city. Most of the bees are workers, and they are all female. Young workers clean the hive, feed the babies, and build wax cells. Older workers fly out to collect nectar and pollen from flowers. When a worker finds a good patch of flowers, she returns to the hive and does a special dance. The dance tells the other bees which way to fly and how far to go.

The queen has one main job, which is laying eggs. In summer, she can lay more than a thousand eggs in a day. Without the work of bees, many fruits and vegetables, such as apples, cherries, and pumpkins, would be much harder to grow.

Dear Diary,

Today our class visited the aquarium in Boston, and I finally saw the penguins up close. I was surprised by how fast they swam. On land they waddled slowly, but in the water they zipped around like tiny rockets. Our guide told us that penguins can't fly, but their wings work like flippers. She also said that almost all wild penguins live in the Southern Hemisphere, so you would never see one at the North Pole.

My favorite was a little penguin named Pebble. He kept diving for fish and then hopping onto a rock to shake off. I took notes, drew three sketches, and asked more questions than anyone else. I can't wait to go back.

An elephant's trunk is one of the most useful body parts in the animal world. It is really a long nose joined with the upper lip, and it has thousands of muscles. Elephants use their trunks to breathe, smell, drink, and grab food. A thirsty elephant sucks water into its trunk and then sprays it into its mouth. On hot days, it may spray water or dust over its back to stay cool.

Trunks are also used for saying hello. Two elephants often touch trunks when they meet, a bit like a handshake. African elephants have two small tips at the end of their trunks, but Asian elephants have only one. Those tips help them pick up things as small as a single peanut.

t: Why Ice Is Lighter Than Water
x:
Most things get smaller when they freeze, but water is different. When water turns into ice, its tiny particles line up in a pattern that takes up more space. That means ice is less dense than liquid water, so it floats. You can see this every time you drop ice cubes into a glass of juice.

This odd fact matters a lot to living things. In winter, a layer of ice forms on top of a lake, and the water below stays liquid. Fish, frogs, and turtles can survive there until spring. If ice sank, lakes could freeze from the bottom up, and many of the animals in them would have nowhere to go. I think it's amazing that something as simple as an ice cube can teach us so much.

You can make your own rainbow with just a glass of water, a sunny window, and a sheet of white paper. First, fill the glass almost to the top. Next, set it on a table near the window so that sunlight passes through the water. Then hold the paper where the light lands, and move it slowly until you see colors appear.

What is happening? Sunlight looks white, but it is really a mix of many colors. When light passes through water, it bends, and each color bends by a slightly different amount. The colors spread out into red, orange, yellow, green, blue, and violet. Real rainbows in the sky form the same way, when sunlight shines through tiny drops of rain.

Last week, Ms. Rivera gave each of us a bar magnet and a tray of small objects. We tested paper clips, coins, a rubber band, a nail, and a plastic spoon. The paper clips and the nail jumped right to the magnet, but the rubber band and the spoon did not move at all. The coins did not stick either, which surprised me.

Ms. Rivera explained that magnets pull on certain metals, such as iron, nickel, and steel. Every magnet has two ends called poles. If you put two north poles together, they push apart. If a north pole faces a south pole, the two magnets pull together. By the end of class, Jamal and I had built a little car that rolled away when we pointed another magnet at it.

Every sound you hear starts with something that vibrates, or moves back and forth very quickly. When you pluck a guitar string, it shakes the air around it. Those shakes pass from one bit of air to the next, like a wave moving through a crowd at a ball game. When the wave reaches your ear, your eardrum vibrates too, and your brain turns that into sound.

Sound can also travel through water and solid things. In fact, it moves faster through water than through air, and even faster through wood or steel. If you put your ear on a table and tap the other end, the knock sounds louder than it does through the air. Out in space, there is almost no air, so there is nothing to carry sound. Astronauts use radios to talk to each other.

Mars is the fourth planet from the Sun, and it is often called the Red Planet. Its color comes from rusty dust that covers much of its surface. Mars is smaller than Earth, and it is much colder. Its air is very thin, so people could not breathe there without special suits.

Mars has some amazing places. Olympus Mons is the tallest volcano in the solar system, and it is more than twice as tall as Mount Everest. Mars also has two tiny moons named Phobos and Deimos. Since the 1990s, NASA has sent several rovers to explore the planet. They have taken pictures, drilled into rocks, and found signs that water once flowed there long ago.

Dear Aunt Maya,

Thank you so much for the telescope you sent for my birthday! Dad and I set it up in the backyard on Saturday night. First, we looked at the Moon, and I could see craters all along its edge. Then we found Jupiter, which looked like a bright little ball. Next to it were four tiny dots in a line. Dad said they were Jupiter's biggest moons, and that Galileo first saw them more than 400 years ago. I wanted to look at Saturn's rings too, but it was too low in the sky that night. I'm keeping a log of everything I see, with the date and time. Maybe someday I'll discover a comet and name it after you.

Love, Sofia

The International Space Station circles Earth about every ninety minutes. That means the astronauts on board see around sixteen sunrises and sunsets every day! The station is about as long as a football field, and people from many countries have lived and worked there since 2000.

Life in space is very different from life at home. Because everything floats, astronauts strap themselves into sleeping bags attached to the walls. They drink from pouches with straws, and they eat food that won't crumble, since crumbs could drift into equipment. To keep their muscles and bones strong, they exercise for about two hours each day. They also run science experiments, take photos of Earth, and talk with students back on the ground.

The Sun may look small in the sky, but it is huge. More than a million Earths could fit inside it. The Sun is a star, just like the tiny points of light we see at night. It looks so much bigger and brighter because it is much closer to us than any other star.

The Sun is a giant ball of hot gases, and its light takes about eight minutes to reach Earth. Without that light and heat, plants could not grow, and our planet would be frozen. People should never look straight at the Sun, even with sunglasses, because it can hurt their eyes. Scientists study it with special telescopes, and they have learned that it will keep shining for billions of years.

Deep under the ground, it is so hot that some rock melts into a thick liquid called magma. Magma is lighter than the solid rock around it, so it slowly rises. Sometimes it collects in a chamber beneath a mountain. When enough pressure builds up, the magma bursts out through an opening, and the volcano erupts. Once magma reaches the surface, it is called lava.

Some volcanoes, like Kilauea in Hawaii, ooze rivers of lava that flow fairly slowly. Others explode and send ash high into the sky. Over time, cooled lava can build new land. In fact, the Hawaiian Islands were formed by volcanoes rising from the floor of the Pacific Ocean, one island at a time.

Imagine you are a tiny drop of water in the ocean. One sunny morning, the Sun warms you, and you rise into the air as an invisible gas. This step is called evaporation. High in the sky, the air is cold, so you cool down and join other drops to form a cloud. That step is called condensation.

As more drops crowd together, the cloud grows heavy. Soon you fall back to the ground as rain, snow, sleet, or hail. This is precipitation. You might land in a river, soak into the soil, or freeze on top of a mountain. Someday, you will flow back to the sea, and the whole trip will start again. The same water has been going around and around on Earth for billions of years.

Plants can't walk, but their seeds still find ways to travel. Some seeds float on the wind. A dandelion seed has a soft, fluffy top that works like a tiny parachute. Maple seeds have wings, so they spin like helicopters as they fall. Other seeds ride along on animals. Burrs have little hooks that catch on fur, socks, and shoelaces.

Coconuts can even travel across the ocean. Their hard shells hold air, so they float for weeks before washing up on a beach. Birds and squirrels help too. They eat berries and nuts, and then they drop or bury the seeds far from the parent plant. When I found a burr stuck to my dog after a hike, I realized she had been helping a plant spread its seeds.

Geologists sort rocks into three main groups. Igneous rocks form when melted rock cools and hardens. Granite and basalt are two examples. Sedimentary rocks form when layers of sand, mud, and tiny shells are pressed together over a very long time. Sandstone and limestone are in this group, and they often hold fossils.

Metamorphic rocks begin as one kind of rock, but heat and pressure deep underground change them into something new. For example, limestone can turn into marble. At the Grand Canyon in Arizona, you can see layers of rock stacked like the pages of a book. Each layer tells part of the story of what the land was like millions of years ago.

In 1804, Meriwether Lewis and William Clark set out from near St. Louis to explore the land west of the Mississippi River. President Thomas Jefferson wanted to learn about the plants, animals, rivers, and people of the West. The group traveled by boat, on foot, and on horseback. They kept careful journals and drew maps along the way.

A young Shoshone woman named Sacagawea joined the group, and she helped them talk with Native American nations they met. After more than a year, the explorers finally reached the Pacific Ocean in 1805. They returned to St. Louis in 1806 with notes about hundreds of plants and animals that were new to them.

Benjamin Franklin was one of the most curious people in American history. He was born in Boston in 1706, but he moved to Philadelphia when he was seventeen. There, he worked as a printer and published a popular yearly book called Poor Richard's Almanack. It was full of weather guesses, jokes, and wise sayings.

Franklin loved science, too. He studied electricity and invented the lightning rod, which helps protect buildings during storms. He also invented bifocal glasses and a stove that heated rooms better than an open fire. Later, he helped write the Declaration of Independence. People still remember him as a writer, scientist, inventor, and leader.

Long ago, a boy named Ahmose lived near the Nile River in ancient Egypt. Every summer, the river flooded and spread rich, dark mud over the fields. When the water went down, Ahmose helped his father plant wheat and barley. His mother baked bread, and his sister wove linen cloth from flax plants.

In the afternoon, Ahmose sometimes went to the river to watch boats carry huge stones to the builders. Their work was slow and hard, but the great pyramids took shape year after year. Scribes wrote on sheets made from papyrus reeds, using little pictures called hieroglyphs. Ahmose hoped that someday he could learn to read them too.

In 1860, sending a letter from Missouri to California could take weeks or even months. The Pony Express promised to do it in about ten days. Young riders carried the mail on fast horses across plains, deserts, and mountains. Every ten to fifteen miles, a rider reached a station where a fresh horse was waiting. He jumped onto the new horse and galloped off again in just a couple of minutes.

The riders traveled day and night, in rain, snow, and heat. However, the Pony Express lasted only about eighteen months. In 1861, a telegraph line was finished that could send messages across the country in minutes. After that, there was no need for horses to race the mail west.

Dear Grandpa,

Greetings from Paris, France! Yesterday, we climbed the Eiffel Tower. We took the stairs to the second level, and then we rode an elevator to the top. From there, the cars looked like ants, and I could see the Seine River winding through the city. Mom said the tower was built for a world's fair in 1889. Today we ate warm croissants for breakfast and visited the Louvre, a huge art museum. I saw the Mona Lisa, but it was smaller than I expected, and there were lots of people in front of it. Tomorrow we're taking a boat ride on the river. I miss you, and I'll bring you a little model of the tower.

Your grandson, Leo

Japan is a country in East Asia made up of thousands of islands. Most people live on the four largest ones, and the biggest of all is called Honshu. Tokyo, the capital, is one of the largest cities in the world. Trains there are famous for being fast and on time. The bullet train can travel at almost 200 miles per hour.

Japan also has quiet gardens, old castles, and tall mountains. Mount Fuji is its highest peak, and on a clear day you can see it from Tokyo. Each spring, cherry trees bloom with pink and white flowers, and families gather in parks to enjoy them. Many people in Japan eat rice, fish, and vegetables, and they often use chopsticks.

A map is a drawing of a place as seen from above. To understand one, you need to read its key, which is sometimes called a legend. The key explains what each symbol means. For example, a small tent might stand for a campground, and a blue line might show a river. Most maps also have a compass rose that shows north, south, east, and west.

Last summer, my cousin Ava and I used a trail map in Yellowstone National Park. We found our lodge, a picnic area, and a path that led to a waterfall. The map's scale showed that one inch stood for one mile, so we could tell how far we had to walk. Thanks to the map, we never got lost, and we made it back before dinner.

The Amazon River flows across South America, mostly through Brazil. It carries more water than any other river on Earth. In fact, it holds more water than the next several biggest rivers combined. During the rainy season, parts of the river spread out so wide that you can't see the other side.

The river runs through the Amazon rainforest, which is the largest rainforest in the world. More kinds of plants and animals live there than almost anywhere else. Pink river dolphins swim in its waters, and colorful parrots, sloths, and monkeys live in the trees. Many people live along the river too. They fish, farm, and travel by boat, since there are very few roads in some parts of the forest.

Our fifth-grade class needed money for a trip to the science museum, so we decided to hold a bake sale. Everyone signed up to bring something. Priya made lemon bars, Marcus brought banana bread, and I baked two dozen oatmeal cookies with my dad. We set up tables in the front hall of the school on Friday morning.

At first, only a few people stopped by, and I was worried. Then the bell rang for lunch, and a long line formed. By two o'clock, we had sold almost everything. We counted the money three times to be sure. We had raised more than enough for the trip, so we gave the extra money to the school library for new books.

In my family, everyone has chores, even my little sister, who is six. Every Sunday night, Mom writes a list on the kitchen whiteboard. My jobs usually include feeding our cat, taking out the trash, and folding the laundry. My brother washes the dishes, and my sister sets the table before dinner.

I used to complain about chores, but now I don't mind them as much. Dad showed me that if I finish them quickly, I have more time to read or play outside. Last month, I also learned to make scrambled eggs, so now I cook breakfast on Saturdays. It feels good to help, and our house runs more smoothly when we all work together.

When I woke up on Tuesday, my room was strangely quiet. I looked out the window and saw that the whole street was covered in snow. Then Mom called up the stairs that school was closed for the day! I ran downstairs, ate a bowl of oatmeal, and pulled on my boots, coat, hat, and mittens.

My friend Nora and her brother met me at the park. We built a snowman with a carrot nose, and then we had a snowball battle that lasted almost an hour. Our fingers grew so cold that we went to Nora's house for hot cocoa. Her mom let us watch a movie, and we stayed warm by the fire. It was the best snow day I can remember.

A picnic is a fun way to spend a sunny afternoon, but it takes a little planning. First, choose a spot, such as a park, a beach, or your own backyard. Next, check the weather so you don't get caught in the rain. Then make a list of food that is easy to carry. Sandwiches, fruit, cheese, and crackers are all good choices, and they won't spill.

Pack a blanket, napkins, and plenty of water. Put cold foods in a cooler with ice so that they stay fresh. When you arrive, find a shady place to spread out your blanket. After you eat, play a game of catch or tag. Before you leave, pick up all your trash, so the park stays clean for the next family.

In 1891, a teacher named James Naismith had a problem. It was winter in Springfield, Massachusetts, and his students were stuck inside with too much energy. He needed a game they could play indoors. Naismith nailed two peach baskets to the railing of a balcony and gave the class a soccer ball. The goal was to toss the ball into the other team's basket.

The first games were a little clumsy. Every time someone scored, a person had to climb up and get the ball out of the basket! Years later, people cut holes in the bottoms of the nets. Basketball spread quickly to other schools, and today it is played by millions of people in countries around the world.

On Saturday morning, I stood on the starting block at my first swim meet. My knees were shaking, and my stomach felt like it was full of butterflies. I looked up at the stands and saw my parents waving a sign with my name on it. Then the whistle blew, and I dove into the cool water.

I swam the fifty-yard freestyle, which is two lengths of the pool. I kicked hard, kept my head down, and breathed every three strokes, just like Coach Lee had taught us. When I touched the wall, I looked at the clock. I didn't win, but I finished third and beat my best time by two seconds. Coach Lee gave me a high five, and I couldn't stop smiling.

Chess is a game for two players, and it has been played for more than a thousand years. Each player begins with sixteen pieces, which are one king, one queen, two rooks, two bishops, two knights, and eight pawns. Each kind of piece moves in its own way. For example, bishops move diagonally, while knights jump in an L shape.

The goal of the game is to trap the other player's king so that it can't escape. This is called checkmate. Good players think several moves ahead, and they try to guess what their opponent will do next. My grandfather taught me to play when I was eight. At first, he won every game, but last week I finally beat him, and he said he was proud of me.

Soccer is the most popular sport in the world. In most countries, people call it football, since players mainly use their feet. A team has eleven players on the field, and only the goalkeeper is allowed to touch the ball with his or her hands during play. The rest of the team must kick, pass, and head the ball toward the other team's goal.

Every four years, teams from many nations compete in the World Cup. The first World Cup was held in Uruguay in 1930. You don't need much to play, though. Kids in cities, villages, and farms play with a ball and two rocks for goalposts. My friends and I play every day after school, and our games often last until it gets dark.

A pinch pot is one of the easiest things to make with clay. First, roll a lump of clay into a smooth ball about the size of an orange. Next, push your thumb into the center, but don't go all the way through. Then pinch the sides gently between your thumb and fingers while you turn the ball in your hand. Keep pinching and turning until the walls are even.

If the clay starts to crack, dip your finger in a little water and smooth it over. When you're happy with the shape, you can press patterns into the sides with a pencil, a shell, or a leaf. Let the pot dry for several days. Finally, paint it with bright colors, and use it to hold paper clips, rings, or coins.

An orchestra is a large group of musicians who play together. The instruments are sorted into four families. The string family includes violins, violas, cellos, and basses. The woodwind family includes flutes, clarinets, oboes, and bassoons. Brass instruments, such as trumpets and tubas, are made of metal and are played by buzzing the lips. The percussion family includes drums, cymbals, and the xylophone.

The conductor stands in front and leads the group with a thin stick called a baton. Last spring, my class went to hear our city's orchestra. When all the instruments played at once, the sound filled the whole hall. I liked the cellos best, so I'm going to try one at school next year.

Last Thursday, a children's book author came to visit our school. She told us that she wrote her first story when she was nine, and it was about a dragon who was afraid of the dark. Her teacher liked it so much that she hung it on the wall. After that, the author never stopped writing.

She showed us how she plans a book. First, she makes a list of ideas in a notebook. Then she writes a messy first draft, and later she fixes it again and again. She said that even famous writers make lots of mistakes, but they keep working until the story feels right. That night, I started my own story about a cat who sails across the ocean in a teacup.

Origami is the art of folding paper into shapes, and its name comes from two Japanese words meaning fold and paper. People in Japan have practiced it for hundreds of years. With just one square sheet and no scissors or glue, a skilled folder can make birds, frogs, flowers, and boats.

One of the most famous designs is the paper crane. In Japan, there is an old tradition that if you fold a thousand cranes, you may be granted a wish. My friend Kenji showed me how to make a crane during recess. My first try was crooked, and its wings were uneven. By the end of the week, though, I had folded twelve cranes, and I hung them over my desk.

Wilbur and Orville Wright ran a bicycle shop in Dayton, Ohio, but they dreamed of flying. For years, they studied birds, built gliders, and tested their ideas in a homemade wind tunnel. They learned how to steer a flying machine by twisting its wings, which was something no one else had figured out.

On December 17, 1903, they were ready. On a windy beach near Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, Orville climbed aboard their airplane, the Flyer. It rose into the air and stayed up for about twelve seconds. That doesn't sound like much, but it was the first powered, controlled airplane flight in history. The brothers made three more flights that day, and Wilbur's longest lasted almost a minute.

A refrigerator doesn't really make cold. Instead, it moves heat out of the box and into the kitchen. Inside the walls and back of a fridge are thin tubes filled with a special liquid. When this liquid turns into a gas, it soaks up heat from the food and air inside. A pump called a compressor then squeezes the gas, and it gives off that heat through coils on the back.

That is why the back of a refrigerator often feels warm. Before people had refrigerators, families kept food cool with blocks of ice in wooden iceboxes. Someone had to deliver new ice every few days. Today, a fridge keeps milk, fruit, and leftovers fresh for days without any ice at all.

Long ago, books were copied by hand, one page at a time. A single book could take months to finish, so books were rare and very expensive. Around 1450, a German metalworker named Johannes Gutenberg built a printing press that used small metal letters. Workers arranged the letters into words, covered them with ink, and pressed paper on top.

With Gutenberg's press, a shop could print hundreds of pages in a day. Soon, printing presses spread across Europe, and books became much cheaper. More people learned to read, and new ideas traveled faster than ever before. Many people think the printing press was one of the most important inventions in history, and I agree with them.

In 1876, Alexander Graham Bell received a patent for the telephone. A few days later, he spoke the first words ever heard over his invention. He called to his helper, Thomas Watson, who was in another room. Bell said, "Mr. Watson, come here, I want to see you." Watson heard the words through the wire and rushed in.

Early telephones were heavy, and they had to be connected by wires. To make a call, you often had to speak to an operator, who plugged your line into the right place. Today, many people carry phones in their pockets that can send photos, play music, and show maps. Still, they all grew out of Bell's simple idea of sending a voice through a wire.
